# A project as a file

One side writes a project out, the other reads it in after reading what it holds. The file is a copy of the project at one moment. Nothing links the two afterwards: a change on one side does not reach the other. A template is the same file with `template` set.

The file is JSON. It begins `{ "aubergine": "project", "format": 1, … }`.

## What a file never holds

- Anything that ran: tasks, what was written on the owner's list, runs and their notes, the log of notes (only the pinned note is in the file), messages.
- Any credential or setting: no token, nothing from the settings file.
- Anything of the computer it was written on: no path, no user name, no data folder, no working copy, no ID. Folders are written as named places, and things inside the file point at each other by references of the file's own (`c1`, `t3`, `e2`). Reading a file in makes new IDs.
- What a terminal showed or did: no screen, no scroll-back, no history, no conversation, no command line.

## Reading a file in

- Nothing is made until the owner has read what the file holds and accepted exactly that text.
- Where each place is on this computer is asked, or left unset. No path from a file is ever used as a path. A terminal with no place starts in the home folder.
- No shell is started unless the owner asks for it, and an agent never is: a terminal that was an agent's is made as a plain shell and says which agent it was meant for.
- Schedules and rules arrive switched off. Tasks start only when the owner starts them.
- A file that is wrong in any way is refused with a sentence, and nothing of it is used.

## The file

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `aubergine` | Says what kind of file this is. |
| `format` | The format of the file. This version writes and reads 1; a later one is refused with a sentence. |
| `template` | True for a template: a project to start others from. |
| `description` | What it is for, in a few sentences. Shown before it is read in. |
| `name` | The name of the project. Whoever reads the file in may choose another. |
| `color` | Its color. |
| `labels` | Pairs of key and value. |
| `places` | The project's folders, as names. Where each is on a computer is asked there. |
| `canvases` | Its canvases, in the order of their tabs. At least one. |
| `workflows` | The workflows it owns and the shared ones its schedules run. Each has a reference (`w1`), `shared` (true if it was shared with every project where the file was written) and `file`: the workflow as a workflow file. |
| `elements` | The saved steps it owns and the shared ones its rules and schedules run. Each has a reference (`e1`), `shared` and `element` (see the step reference). |
| `rules` | Its rules. |
| `schedules` | Its schedules. |
| `leftOut` | What could not be written into the file, each in a sentence. |

Fields this version does not know are kept when a file is read in, and written out again when that project is written to a file.

## A place

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `name` | The name of the place: a word, such as `main` or `docs`. Terminals name it. |
| `hint` | The last part of the folder's path where the file was written, to help whoever is asked where the place is. Never used as a path. |
| `default` | True for the place new terminals start in. |

## A canvas

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `ref` | Its reference inside this file, such as `c1`. |
| `name` | The name on its tab. |
| `color` | The color of its tab. |
| `labels` | Pairs of key and value. |
| `frames` | Its frames: a rectangle, a label and a color each. |
| `nodes` | Its nodes, in the order they are drawn: a rectangle, a color, and the terminal to make there. |

## A terminal, on a node

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `ref` | Its reference inside this file, such as `t1`. Rules and schedules name it. |
| `name` | What the terminal is called. |
| `tags` | Its tags. |
| `note` | Its pinned note. Left out of a template unless the owner kept the notes. |
| `place` | The place it starts in. Null: no place; it starts in the home folder of whoever reads the file in. |
| `subfolder` | A folder below that place. |
| `agent` | The agent it ran, by its kind. It is made as a plain shell and says which agent it was meant for: reading a file in never starts an agent. |
| `environment` | The kind of place it worked in. Said on the terminal; nothing is prepared by reading the file in. |

## A rule

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `event` | What sets it off. |
| `action` | What it does: `{"kind":"notify"}`, or `{"kind":"run-element","element":"e1","on":{"terminal":"t1"}}` (or `{"canvas":"c1"}` for a new terminal there). It arrives switched off. |

## A schedule

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `name` | What the schedule is called. It arrives switched off. |
| `time` | The time of day, on this computer's clock and in its time zone. |
| `days` | The days of the week it runs on. |
| `what` | What it runs: `{"element":"e1"}` or `{"workflow":"w1"}`. |
| `where` | Where: `{"terminal":"t1"}`, or `{"canvas":"c1"}` for a new terminal there. |
| `task` | What the agent is told to do. |

## Comparing a file with a project

A file kept somewhere, in a repository for instance, can be compared with a project: what the file has that the project lacks, what the project has that the file lacks, and what both have differently.

```sh
aubergine project diff garden-site.project.json --project "Garden site"
```

Without `--project` it is the project chosen with `aubergine project use`, else the first. `--text` also prints how the texts differ, line by line (a summary, the task of a schedule, what an agent is told by a step or a workflow): lines that begin with `-` are only here, lines that begin with `+` are only in the file. `--json` prints the answer as data, with the same field names as the route `POST /v1/projects/<id>/file/compare`.

**It changes nothing.** No state, nothing made, nothing started, nothing written. There is no command that makes a project match a file: applying a file to a project that is there is not built.

**How it compares.** The project is written out as a file is, by the code that writes files, and the two are compared in that shape. So only what a file holds is compared, and a template without summaries is compared without them (the answer says so).

**How things are matched: by name, never by an ID and never by their order.**

- A canvas by its name. A terminal by its name on its canvas. A frame by its label on its canvas.
- A place by its name. A schedule, a workflow and a saved step by their names.
- A rule has no name in a file. It is all of what it says (what sets it off, what it does, and the step and the terminal or canvas it names, by their names), so a rule is on both sides or on one, and never "differs".
- A thing that was renamed shows as two lines: one only in the file, one only here. Nothing says that the two are one thing.
- Where a name is on a side more than once, and the things of that name are not exactly the same on both sides, they **cannot be told apart**: the line says so, and nothing is guessed from the order they stand in. Nothing on a canvas that could not be told apart is compared.

**What counts as different.** The name, color and labels of the project and the order of its canvases; a place and whether new terminals start there; the color and labels of a canvas; of a terminal its color, tags, summary, where it starts (a place and a folder below it, never a path), the agent it was meant for, what it works in, and whether it was moved or resized; of a frame its color and whether it was moved or resized; of a schedule its time, days, what it runs, where, and its task; of a workflow and a saved step their content, and whether they are shared with every project. A terminal or a frame counts as moved or resized when it is more than 1 away from where the file has it; no numbers are printed.

**What is not compared**, because a file does not hold it: what ran (tasks, runs, logs of notes, messages), fields, links, themes, whether a rule or a schedule is switched on, where a workflow or a step came from, the order terminals are drawn in, parked terminals, the hint of a place, and any path of this computer. The last line of every answer says so, so that "matches" is not read as "the same in everything".

**It ends with** 0 when the project matches the file, 1 when they differ, and 2 when nothing was compared: the file is wrong or cannot be read, the project is not found, or the server does not answer. A file that is wrong in any way is refused whole, with the same sentence as when it is read in.

An example:

```
The file compared with the project “Garden site”. Nothing was changed.

Canvases
  differs: “Build”: color (purple in the file, teal here)

Terminals on “Build”
  only in the file: “shell”
  only here: “scratch”
  differs: “builder”: tags (agent in the file, agent, slow here); summary; moved

Rules
  only here: when a task needs you: notify

1 only in the file, 2 only here, 2 differ.
To see how the texts differ, line by line: --text
A file does not hold what ran (tasks, runs, logs of notes, messages), fields, links, themes, whether a rule or a schedule is switched on, where a thing came from, the order terminals are drawn in, parked terminals, or any path of this computer: none of that was compared.
```

## Bounds

A file is at most 400000 characters. It may hold 50 canvases, 200 nodes and 100 frames on a canvas, 300 terminals in all, 20 places, 50 workflows, 100 steps, 50 rules and 50 schedules.
